senses: to beg, solicit, pray to (someone) for (something) (with two accusatives)
la:verb:rogo.html:
rŏgo, āvi, ātum, 1 (
inf. paragog. rogarier, : rogassint, for rogaverint,), v. a.
etym. dub.; perh. for progo; kindr. with Sanscr. prac, to ask, whence also precor and procus, but referred by Corss. to the same root with Sanscr. rgus, straight; Gr. ὀρέγω; Lat. rego, rex, rogus, Krit. Beit. p. 93
, to ask, question, interrogate one about a thing.
Lit.
In gen. (so generally throughout ante-class. Lat.; less. freq. in Cic.; syn.: percontor, sciscitor, quaero), constr. aliquem aliquid, or simply aliquem, aliquid, with de, a rel.-clause, or absol. (cf. Zumpt, Gram. § 393). (a) Aliquem aliquid (class. only with acc. of neutr. pron. or adj., or with sententiam;v.infra, B. 1.): aliud te rogo,: haud istuc te rogo,: quin tu id me rogas,: hoc te rogo, quos locos adisti?; cf.: rogare hoc unum te volo,: dic mihi hoc, quod te rogo,; ; ; et saep.; : ego patriam te rogo, quae sit tua,; cf.: hanc (colubram) alia cum rogaret causam facinoris, Respondit, etc.,. —
Aliquem or aliquid: quos rogo,: quem ego igitur rogem?: ecquem hominem tu novisti? te rogo,; men' or me rogas? also, rogas me? in colloq. lang., do you ask that of me? how can you ask? what do you mean by asking that? Eu. Quid ego facerem? Ch. Quid tu faceres? men' rogas? requireres, Rogitares, etc., ; ; ; ; ; ; cf.: quid me istud rogas? inquam: Stoicos roga,: hoc quod rogo responde,; ; ; ; ; .—
With de: jam de istoc rogare omitte,; so, de istac virgine,: de te ipso,.—
With interrog.-clause: rogant me servi, quo eam?: roga ipsum, quemadmodum ego eum Arimini acceperim, ap. : quodsi me populus Romanus forte roget, cur Non, etc.,: quae sit, rogo,: rogo, num quid velit,: rogavi pervenissetne Agrigentum?: unde venis? et Quo tendis? rogat et respondet,: quid verum atque decens curo et rogo,. — (ε) Absol.: prius respondes quam rogo,: roganti respondebo,: non edepol nunc, ubi terrarum, sim, scio, si quis roget,: quin tu ergo rogas?: Ty. Quid ego deliqui? He. Rogas? ; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. : etiam rogas?

do you dare to ask? ; ; ; (v. etiam). — Particularly as subst.: numquam nobis ad rogatum respondent,. —

In partic. (class. in all per.).
Publicists' t. t.
Rogare aliquem (sententiam), to ask one for his opinion or vote: Racilius Marcellinum primum rogavit. Is sententiam dixit, ut, etc.... Postea Racilius de privatis me primum sententiam rogavit,: quos priores sententiam rogabat,. — Pass.: cum omnes ante me rogati gratias Caesari egissent, ego rogatus mutavi meum consilium,: scito primum me non esse rogatum sententiam,: primus rogatus sententiam,: is enim primus rogatus sententiam,; : propter ipsam rem, de quā sententiae rogantur, consultabitur,. —
Rogare populum or legem, or absol., prop., to ask the people about a law; hence, in gen., to bring the plan of a law before the people for their approval; to propose a law, introduce a bill: in aes incidi jubebitis credo illa legitima: consules populum jure rogaverunt populusque jure scivit,; cf.: T. Quinctius Crispinus consul populum jure rogavit populusque jure scivit in foro pro rostris ... quicumque post hanc legem rogatam rivos, specus, etc., an old legal formula ap. : plebem,: legem,; ; cf.: quae (leges) non in perpetuum rogentur,. — Absol.: ego hanc legem, uti rogas, jubendam censeo,; . — Impers. pass.: nunc rogari, ut populus consules creet,.—
Rogare populum magistratum, and simply magistratum, to propose a magistrate to the people for their choice, to offer him for election: factum senatus consultum, ut duo viros aediles ex patribus dictator populum rogaret,; cf.: L. Trebonius tribunus plebis rogationem tulit, ut qui plebem Romanam tribunos plebi rogaret, is usque eo rogaret dum, etc.,: (Caesar) volet, ut consules roget praetor vel dictatorem dicat: quorum neutrum jus est,; cf.: praetores, cum ita rogentur, ut collegae consulibus sint, etc.,: hodieque in legibus magistratibusque rogandis usurpatur idem jus,: comitia consulibus rogandis habuit,; ; ; cf. ; : Calpurnius Romam ad magistratus rogandos proficiscitur,.— Absol.: mortuo rege Pompilio Tullum Hostilium populus regem, interrege rogante, comitiis curiatis creavit,.—
Milit. t. t.: rogare milites sacramento, qs. to ask the soldiers if they will take and keep an oath, i. e. to bind them by an oath, administer an oath to them, ; ; fin.; 40, 26; cf. . —
Jurid. t. t., to ask a person if he will promise something in making an agreement; to propose a stipulation: quod fere novissimā parte pactorum ita solet inseri: rogavit Titius, spopondit Maevius, haec verba non tantum pactionis loco accipiuntur sed etiam stipulationis,; ; ; .
Transf., to ask, beg, request, solicit one for a thing (so predominantly in the class. per.; syn.: posco, oro, obsecro, ambio, capto); constr. aliquem (rarely ab aliquo) aliquid, aliquem, aliquid, with ut, ne, or absol.
With acc.: quā confidentiā rogare argentum me tantum audes, Impudens? Quin si egomet totus veneam, vix recipi potis est, Quod tu me rogas,: hoc te vehementer etiam atque etiam rogo,: nefas sit tale aliquid et facere rogatum et rogare ... Haec igitur lex in amicitiā sanciatur, ut neque rogemus res turpes nec faciamus rogati,: otium divos rogat, Hor. c. 2, 16, 1; cf.: divitias deos,: a Metello missionem,: ut ab avunculo rogetur Aethiops,: rogo te, vos, etc., parenthet.: rogo te, videte, quibus hominibus negotium detis, etc.,: rogo vos, quis potest sine offulā vivere?: illae Priami rogantis Achillem preces,: taurum de aquā per fundum ejus ducenda rogabo, : ambiuntur, rogantur,are asked for their votes,: etiamsi precario essent rogandi,: transisse Rhenum sese non suā sponte sed rogatum et arcessitum a Gallis,; cf.: ille ab Sardis rogatus ad causam accesserat,: in proximum annum consulatum peteres, vel potius rogares ... a quā (Galliā) nos tum, cum consulatus petebatur, non rogabatur, etc.,was not begged for,: abii ad praetorem, rogo syngraphum: Datur mihi,: aquam,: legatos ad Caesarem mittunt rogatum auxilium,; cf. : aliquid ab aliquo (rare),; : cultrum, securim, etc. ... Quae utenda vasa semper vicini rogant,ask for, borrow,; ; .—
With ut or ne (so most freq.): scitin' quid ego vos rogo? mihi ut praeconium detis,; : id ut facias, vehementer te rogo,: etiam atque etiam te rogo atque oro, ut eum juves,: rogat et orat Dolabellam, ut, etc.,: cum rogat et prece cogit Scilicet ut, etc.,; Caes. ap. , C, 1; : videbatur rogare, scalas ut darem utendas sibi,that I would lend,; ; ; .— With a simple final clause without ut: Caesar consolatus rogat, finem orandi faciat,; ; ; ; and very freq. ap. ; e. g. 1, 2, 1; 1, 5, 8; 1, 20, 24; 2, 5, 2; 3, 2, 6; 5, 19, 8; 7, 6, 11; 8, 17, 6.—With ne: rogat frater, ne abeas longius,: ac te illud primum rogabo, ne quid invitus meā causā facias,. —
Absol.: neque enim ego sic rogabam, ut petere viderer, quia familiaris esset meus (Plancus), etc., did not solicit in such a way as to, etc., (differing from α): in blandiendo, rogando lenis et summissa (vox),: patrem et filium pro vitā rogantes,; cf.: pro aliquo,; .—
Esp., to invite, ask a visit from any one: Tertia aderit, modo ne Publius rogatus sit,: Pomponiam Terentia rogat,— With ad or in and acc.: ad Palatium,: in senatum,: ad convivium,: ad nuptias,: in consilium,.—
Prov.: malo emere quam rogare, of a thing that does not cost much,I had rather buy than borrow it,; cf. supra, α and β. —
In gen., to seek, bring, take: aquam hinc de proximo rogabo,: hujus (purpurae) exemplum aliunde rogabo, tibi quod ostendam (cf.: exemplum quaeritent, etc., in context),.

la:noun:rogus.html:
rŏgus, i, m. (collat. form rŏgum, i, n., Afran. ap. ; cf. Com. Rel. p. 153 Rib.).
A funeral pile (syn. bustum): ROGVM ASCIA NE POLITO, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. ; : aliena rogorum insuper exstructa,; : in rogum illatus,: ascendere in rogum,: aliquem in rogum imponere,: rogum exstruere,: rogo illata,: portari in rogum,; ; ; et saep.— Poet.: diffugiunt avidos carmina sola rogos,i. e. escape destruction,.—
Transf., the grave: obserat umbrosos lurida porta rogos,

la:noun:Roma.html:
Rōma, ae, f., = Ῥώμη,
the city of Rome, founded in the second year of the seventh Olympiad (B. C. 753), ; ; worshipped as a goddess in a particular temple,; ; ; cf.: Roma ferox,: princeps urbium,: ROMAE AETERNAE,; ; : ROMAE ET AVGVSTO,.—Hence,
Rōmānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Rome, Roman: forum, v. h. v.: populus Romanus (always in this order; abbreviated P. R.); v. populus: Juno, the Roman (opp. Argiva), : lingua Romana, i. e. Latin, Laurea Tull. poët. ap. ; ; ; : Romana lingua,, praef. § 2; ; Treb. Poll. Trig. Tyr. 28, 2; : litterae Romanae (= litterae Latinae),: sermo Romanus,; ; ; 123: auctores. ; : ludi, also called ludi magni, the most ancient in Rome, annually celebrated on the 4th of September, ; ; ; fin. et saep.: Romano more,in the Roman manner, plainly, openly, candidly, frankly,; ; .—As subst.: Rōmānus, i, m.
Sing. collect., = the Romans, ; . —
The Roman (sc. imperator), : Romanus sedendo vincit (cf. Q. Fabius Maximus),.—
Plur.: Romani,the Romans,; et saep.— Adv.: Rōmānē, in the Roman manner, plainly, candidly, frankly, etc., . — Hence, Rōmānĭtas, ātis, f., Romanism, the Roman way or manner, .—
Rōmānĭcus, a, um, adj., Roman: aratra, juga,i. e. made in Rome,: fiscinae,, § 3.—
Rō-mānĭensis, e, adj., of Rome, Roman: sal,.—Collat. form Rōmānen-ses, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. Corinthienses, p. 61, 1 Müll. —
Rōmānŭlus, a, um, adj. dim., of Rome, Roman: Porta, Müll.—
Rōmŭlĭus or Rō-mĭlĭus, a, um, adj., of Rome, Roman: tribus, Müll.; Fest. pp. 270 and 271 ib.; .

rŏgātor, ōris, m.
rogo
.
In publicists' lang., *
One who proposes a law to the people, the proposer of a law, presenter of a bill: legum, Lucil. ap. (v. infra, II. A.). —
An officer in the votingcomitia who asked the people for their votes, a collector of votes, a polling-clerk, : justus comitiorum rogator,; : vos rogatores, vos diribitores, vos custodes fuisse tabularum,.—
Transf., in gen., *
One who makes a proposal, a proposer (in allusion to the signif. I. A.): haec epistula non suasoris est sed rogatoris,, B, 9. —
A beggar, mendicant, ; .

la:noun:rogatio.html:
rŏgātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
.
Publicists' t. t., an inquiry of the people as to whether they will decree this or that, a proposal to the people for passing a law or decree, a proposed law or decree, a bill: quae (rogatio) de Pompeio a Gellio et a Lentulo consulibus lata est,was proposed, presented, introduced,: quibus lege aut rogatione civitas aut libertas erepta sit, Halm ad loc.: rogationem ferre de aliquo,: in aliquem,: ad populum,: ad plebem,: in dissuasione rogationis ejus, quae contra coloniam Narbonensem ferebatur,: Piso lator rogationis idem erat dissuasor,: rogationem promulgare,; cf.: promulgantur uno eodemque tempore rogationes ab eodem tribuno de meā pernicie et de provinciis consulum,; : suasit rogationem,recommended, spoke in favor of it,; : intercedere rogationi,to oppose it,: rogationem accipere,to accept it,; for which: rogationes jubere (opp. antiquare),: per vim rogationem perferre,to carry through,: cum provocatione rogationem pertulit,: recitare rogationis carmen,. — The formula made use of in such a rogation runs thus, in : velitis jubeatis uti, etc. (here follows the proposed law; at the close): haec ita uti dixi ita vos Quirites rogo.—
Transf., in gen.,
A question, interrogation, only as a figure of speech: rogatio atque huic finitima quasi percontatio,; . —
An asking, demanding; a prayer, entreaty, request (very rare): ego Curtium non modo rogatione sed etiam testimonio tuo diligo,; : injusta amici,; .

la:noun:robur.html:
rōbur (rōbor, v. Lachm.; also an older form rōbus, ; ; cf. Paul. ex Müll.), ŏris, n.
cf. Sanscr. radh-as, abundance; Gr. ῥώννυμι for ῥώθνυμι, to strengthen, ῥώμη
,
a very hard kind of oak (cf.: quercus, ilex),; ; ; 16, 40, 76, § 204; 16, 40, 77, § 218.— Hence,
Lit.
In gen., a very hard kind of tree or wood: morsus roboris,i. e. of the wild olive, (a little before: foliis oleaster amaris Hic steterat); so of the same,; cf.: solido de robore myrtus,: annoso validam robore quercum,i. e. of an old and sturdy trunk,; so, annoso robore quercus,: antiquo robore quercus,with ancient trunk,: Massyla, i. e. citri,; also, Maurorum,.—
Absol., usu., an oak-tree, an oak in gen.: fixa est pariter cum robore cervix,i. e. was pinned fast to the oak,: agitata robora pulsant (delphines),.—
Oak-wood, oak: naves totae factae ex robore,; cf.: (sapiens) non est e saxo sculptus aut e robore dolatus,; and with this cf. . — Poet.: illi robur et aes triplex Circa pectus erat,; cf.: o saxis nimirum et robore nati!. —
Transf.
Of things made of oak or of any other hard wood.
In gen.: Lacedaemonii cottidianis epulis in robore accumbunt,i. e. on oaken, hard benches,.— So of the wooden horse before Troy: sacrum,; of a lance: ferro praefixum,; ; ; of a club, ; et saep.: aratri,i. e. the oaken plough,; .—
In partic., the lower and stronger part of the prison at Rome, built by Servius Tullius, was called Robur (also Tullianum): Robus in carcere dicitur is locus, quo praecipitatur maleficorum genus, quod ante arcis robusteis includebatur, Paul. ex Fest. s. v. robum, p. 264 Müll.: in robore et tenebris exspiret,: robur et saxum minitari,; : verbera, carnifices, robur,; (v. carcer and Tullianum).—
Hardness, strength, firmness, vigor, power (cf. vires; v. Fabri ad ).
Lit.: duri robora ferri,; so, ferri,: saxi,: navium,: omnia pariter crescunt et robora sumunt, gain strength,

; ; cf.: qui si jam satis aetatis atque roboris haberet, ipse pro Sex. Roscio diceret,: paululum jam roboris accessit aetati,: solidaeque suo stant robore vires,; : si quod est robur,.—

Trop., power, strength, force, vigor (very freq.): alter virtutis robore firmior quam aetatis,: in animi excelsi atque invicti magnitudine ac robore,; so, animi (with magnitudo),; : robur incredibile animi,: quantum in cujusque animo roboris est ac nervorum,: multo plus firmamenti ac roboris,; so (with firmamentum) ; (with firmitas) : hi tot equites Romani quid roboris hujus petitioni attulerunt?: pectus robore fultum,: te mea robora fallunt,: velocitate pari, robore animi virumque praestanti,: verba quanti roboris plena,: qui robur aliquod in stilo fecerint,; cf.: robur oratorium adicere sententiis,; : illi robur et aes triplex Circa pectus erat,; cf.: O saxis nimirum et robore nati,. —
Authority: nostrarum constitutionum, prooem. 6.—
Concr., the strongest, most effective, or best part, the pith, kernel, strength of any thing; of soldiers, the flower of the troops, choice troops, etc. (freq. and class.): versaris in optimorum civium vel flore vel robore,: et robur et suboles militum interiit, Asin. ap. ; cf.: quod fuit roboris, duobus proeliis interiit,: quod roboris ea provincia habuerat,; : senatūs robur,. — Plur.: tunc C. Flavius Pusio, Cn. Titinnius, C. Maecenas, illa robora populi Romani,: haec sunt nostra robora,; ; ; ; 22, 6; 23, 16; 25, 6 init.: robora pubis,; : ingentia robora virorum,: conferta robora virorum,: betae, i. e. stalks, Col. poët. 10, 326. — Of a place, a stronghold: quod coloniam virium et opum validam robur ac sedem bello legisset,.—Absol.: robus, the name of an excellent kind of wheat: quoniam et pondere et nitore praestat,.

rŏta, ae, f.
kindred with Sanscr. ratha, chariot, and Germ. Rad (cf.rotundus), wheel
,
a wheel.
Lit.: pro rotā me uti licet,; cf.: vorsutior es quam rota figularis,: orbes rotarum,; : axes rotarum,: radiata,: aurea curvatura summae rotae, Ov M. 2, 108: aquaria,: ne currente rotā funis eat retro, while the wheel (in a hoisting machine) hurries forward, et saep.—
In partic.
A potter's wheel (cf. supra, figularis): amphora coepit Institui: currente rotā cur urceus exit?; so, Cumana,: Aristarchus invenit rotam figuli, cujus circuitu vasa formantur,.—
A wheel for torture (τροχός, among the Greeks): in rotam beatam vitam non escendere,: cervicem circumactu rotae frangere,; ; , p. 243; .—Ixion's wheel, ; ; ; et saep.—
A roller: aliquid subjectis rotis traicere,: propellere,; .—
Poet., transf.
(Pars pro toto.) A car, chariot: si rota defuerit, tu pede carpe viam, Ov.A. A. 2,230; cf. (opp. pedibus) ; so ; (3, 20), 26; 4 (5), 10, 42: subdiderat rotas,; ; ; . —Of the span of horses: Cynthia fraternis afflata rotis,.—
Of things in the shape of a wheel or disk.
The disk of the sun: solis rota,; ; cf.: flammea Phoebi,; and simply rota, Enn. ap. ; .—
A kind of sea-fish, ; .—
Trop., a wheel: fortunae rotam pertimescere,i. e. fickleness, inconstancy,; cf.: versatur celeri Fors levis orbe rotae,; (10); ; .—Poet.: imparibus vecta Thalia rotis,i. e. in elegiac metre,; so, disparibus (elegorum) rotis,: jactor, crucior, agitor, stimulor, vorsor in amoris rotā miser, on the rack of love (cf. I. A. 2. b. supra), .

Transf.
In gen., of objects having a similar shape, the curved point of a vine-dresser's billhook, ; of a plough,; of hammers,; of lamps,; of an island,.—
Esp. freq., the curved end of a ship's prow, a ship's beak; sing.: neque his (navibus) nostrae rostro nocere poterant,; so ; ; ; ; ; : navis, cui argenteum aut aureum rostrum est,; —Plur., Auct. B. Scip. 2, 14, 31.— *
Trop.: aut curtum sermone rotato Torqueat enthymema,round, compact, concise,: sic ordinem fati rerum aeterna series rotat,.—
Neutr., = rotari, to turn or roll round, to revolve (very rare): parte ex aliā, quā saxa rotantia late Impulerat torrens, Serv. (cf.: volventia plaustra,); so of a peacock spreading its tail out like a wheel,.

Lit., dew: herbae gemmantes rore recenti,; cf. : ros si non cadit,: nocturnum excipere rorem,; cf.: rore mero jejunia pavit,: gelidus,: pecori gratissimus,; : caelestis,: vitreus, et saep.— Plur.: gelidos rores, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 8, 14: cadunt rores,: roribus,; : quod inter aquam et rorem interest,. —

In gen.: sapiens Fortis et in se ipse totus, teres atque rotundus,: illa rotunda et undique circumcisa,.—
In partic., of speech (opp. rough, unpolished), round, well turned, smooth, polished, elegant (in Cic. with quasi or ut ita dicam added; but v.infra, adv. b.): erat verborum et delectus elegans et apta et quasi rotunda constructio,; cf.: Thucydides praefractior nec satis, ut ita dicam, rotundus,: Graiis dedit ore rotundo Musa loqui,; celeris ac rotunda distributio,: rotunda volubilisque sententia,: rotundi numeri (with brevis),: verba,.—Hence, adv.: rŏtun-dē. *

U.C. 686, carried through a law that fourteen rows of seats in the theatre next to those of the senators should be appropriated to the knights, ; ; Ascon. ap. Cornel. p. 784; ; ; .
